title: 10 Christmas Traditions EVERYONE Forgot (Bring These Back This Year)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, last Christmas my grandson spent the whole afternoon on his phone, his sister on hers, and their parents on the couch watching a game. Nobody talked. Nobody sang. And after everybody left, I sat in my kitchen and I thought, when did we stop doing all the things that made Christmas feel like Christmas? Because it wasn't the presents. It was never the presents.
scenes.caption: NOBODY TALKED

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you ten Christmas traditions that almost everybody forgot. The ones my mother and Grandma Pearl did every single year. They cost almost nothing, and every one of them still works today. Pick two or three for this year, honey, and watch what happens to your house.
scenes.caption: TEN FORGOTTEN TRADITIONS

scenes.text: Tradition number one. The Advent candle. On the first Sunday of December, my mother set four candles in a ring of pine branches on the kitchen table. Every Sunday night after supper, we lit one more, my father read a few lines from the Bible, and we sang one carol. Four Sundays, four candles, and by the last one we could hardly sit still.
scenes.caption: ONE MORE EVERY SUNDAY

scenes.text: How to do it today. Four plain candles from the dollar store, branches from the yard, and fifteen minutes on Sunday night with the phones in another room. Read something, sing one song, even badly. My grandchildren rolled their eyes the first year. Now they're the ones who remind me.
scenes.caption: PHONES IN ANOTHER ROOM

scenes.text: Tradition number two. Caroling. The Saturday before Christmas, our church choir walked the streets of Mansfield in the snow, stopping at the houses of the old people and the shut-ins. Danny and I went with our mittens and a thermos of cocoa. Old Mr. Kessler cried every year when we sang Silent Night on his porch. He lived alone after the war took his son.
scenes.caption: SILENT NIGHT ON THE PORCH

scenes.text: Today, honey, you don't need a choir. Take the children to the house of one neighbor who lives alone, ring the bell, and sing two carols. Bring a plate of cookies. That's it. I promise you, it will be the only visit they remember that whole December.
scenes.caption: TWO CAROLS AND A PLATE

scenes.text: Tradition number three. Writing Christmas letters. Real ones, on paper, with a stamp. My mother sat at the kitchen table every evening in December writing to cousins in Pennsylvania, her old school friends, and my father's army buddies. Each letter was a whole page, in her round handwriting. And when the replies came, she read them out loud at supper.
scenes.caption: A WHOLE PAGE

scenes.text: Do it this year, sweetheart. Pick five people who matter and write each one a real letter. Not a printed card with a photo. A page in your own hand, telling them one thing you remember about them. I write mine on the first week of December. Some of those people are gone now, and their families have told me they kept my letters.
scenes.caption: THEY KEPT MY LETTERS

scenes.text: Tradition number four. Reading aloud on Christmas Eve. Every year, my father read The Night Before Christmas to us in front of the tree, in his big deep voice, and Luke chapter two, the shepherds and the angels. He did the voices. He did Santa's laugh. We knew every word, and we'd say them along with him under our breath.
scenes.caption: HE DID THE VOICES

scenes.text: Today, honey, turn off the television at seven o'clock on Christmas Eve, and have the oldest person in the house read to everybody. Use the same book every year, so it becomes yours. The year after my father died, Danny read it in his place, and halfway through we all had to stop because nobody could see the page.
scenes.caption: THE SAME BOOK EVERY YEAR

scenes.text: Tradition number five. The extra stocking. My mother hung one more stocking than we had people. All December, every time we went to the store, we put something in it. A pair of socks. A bar of soap. An orange. A pencil. On Christmas Eve we took it to the Salvation Army, for a child we'd never meet.
scenes.caption: ONE MORE STOCKING

scenes.text: This one I want you to do this year, sweetheart. It teaches children something no present can. Let them choose what goes in, and let them carry it to the drop-off themselves. Every church, every shelter in America will take it. My grandson filled one at six years old, and he asked me why the other boy didn't have a daddy to buy him things. That was the best Christmas lesson I ever saw.
scenes.caption: THE BEST LESSON

scenes.text: Tradition number six. The Christmas Eve walk. After supper, my father put on his hat and said, let's go look at the lights. And the four of us walked around the neighborhood in the cold, looking at every window, every candle, every tree. Then we came home to cocoa, and that was the only night we were allowed to stay up past ten.
scenes.query: family walking Christmas lights night snow
scenes.caption: LET'S GO LOOK AT THE LIGHTS

scenes.text: Bundle up the whole family and do it. Thirty minutes, no phones, just walking and pointing and saying, look at that one. If it's too cold, pile everybody in the car with a thermos of cocoa and drive slowly through the best neighborhood in town. My grandchildren call it the light tour, and they won't let me skip it.
scenes.caption: THE LIGHT TOUR

scenes.text: Tradition number seven. An orange in the toe of the stocking. In the nineteen thirties, an orange in December was a luxury, and Grandma Pearl got one every Christmas of her childhood and nothing else. So she put an orange in the toe of every stocking for the rest of her life, and my mother did it, and I still do it. It's how we remember that we didn't always have so much.
scenes.caption: WE DIDN'T ALWAYS HAVE SO MUCH

scenes.text: Put one in every stocking this year, honey, right down in the toe. And when the children ask why, tell them about the little girl in nineteen thirty-one who woke up on Christmas morning, found one orange in her stocking, and thought she was the richest girl in Ohio. That little girl was my grandmother. Every orange is a story, if somebody tells it.
scenes.caption: THE RICHEST GIRL IN OHIO

scenes.text: Tradition number eight. Keeping Christmas until the sixth of January. Today the tree goes out on the twenty-sixth, like the party is over. But Grandma Pearl kept the tree, the candles and the music going for the twelve days of Christmas, and on the sixth we had one more little party with the last of the cookies before the decorations came down. Christmas wasn't one day. It was twelve.
scenes.caption: IT WAS TWELVE

scenes.text: Try it this year. Leave the tree up until the sixth of January. Keep one candle lit at supper every night of the twelve days. And on the sixth, have a little party, just the family, with the last of the cookies, and let the children take the ornaments down and wrap them one by one. It turns the saddest day of the year into one more celebration.
scenes.caption: ONE MORE CELEBRATION

scenes.text: Tradition number nine. Thank-you notes before New Year's. My mother sat us down on the twenty-seventh with a stack of note cards, and we couldn't play with a single new toy until we'd written to every aunt and uncle who sent something. Three sentences. Thank you, what I'll do with it, and that I love you. I hated it then. Now I know it's why my aunts loved us so much.
scenes.caption: THREE SENTENCES

scenes.text: Give your children plain note cards and a good pen, honey, and sit down with them and write your own notes at the same time. They'll grumble. Let them. One day an aunt will tell your daughter she kept every note she ever sent, in a drawer, tied with a ribbon. My Aunt Ruth, the one I was named for, did exactly that, and her daughter gave them back to me after the funeral.
scenes.caption: TIED WITH A RIBBON

scenes.text: And tradition number ten, the one I hold closest. The empty chair. When somebody in the family was gone, away at war, or passed on that year, my mother set their place at the Christmas table anyway. A plate, a glass, a candle. And before grace, each of us said one thing we remembered about them. In nineteen sixty-eight, the empty chair was Danny's, and that year we said a prayer instead.
scenes.caption: THE EMPTY CHAIR

scenes.text: Do it this year if you've lost someone, honey. It doesn't make Christmas sadder. It makes it fuller. The children learn who came before them, and the person you miss gets to be at the table one more time.
scenes.caption: ONE MORE TIME

scenes.text: And here's one more small tradition to go with it. Keep a Christmas book. A plain notebook that comes out every December. Every year, write down who was at the table, what you ate, what the children got, and one funny thing somebody said. My mother started ours in nineteen forty-six. I have it on my shelf, and reading it is like having all of them in the room again.
scenes.caption: A CHRISTMAS BOOK

scenes.text: So there they are. The Advent candles. Caroling for one neighbor. Real letters. Reading aloud on Christmas Eve. A stocking for a stranger. The walk to see the lights. An orange in the toe. Twelve days, not one. Thank-you notes. And the empty chair. None of them cost more than a few dollars. All of them are worth more than anything under the tree.
scenes.caption: WORTH MORE THAN PRESENTS

scenes.text: Now tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Which tradition did your family have that nobody does anymore? I read every one, and some of yours might end up in a video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID YOUR FAMILY DO?
